articles.text: Noctis is an adorable, intelligent, 4-year-old cat with a curious mind and a playful spirit. He loves interactive wand play and will happily jump, pounce, and stalk toys with impressive focus—it’s a bit like watching a nature documentary unfold in your living room! You’ll be smitten by his adorable trills (when he’s pleased) and grunts (when he’s displeased). He’s on a special diet to support his digestive health and will need to remain indoors because he has feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), which is easily managed and doesn’t shorten his lifespan. Affectionate and social, this little house panther enjoys soft petting and cuddles in moderation. He’s confident, and loves attention, but he can become overstimulated if petting goes on too long. An adopter with some cat experience who’s comfortable reading body language and redirecting him with toys will help him thrive. Adopt Noctis through Cat Town. When he’s not playing, Noctis enjoys following his people around and keeping a close eye on everything you’re doing. This sweet black cat will greet you at the door when you come home! Noctis would do best in a household where he has space to explore, plenty of daily stimulation, and he may do well with another cat. He’s neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV-negative, Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@ cattownoakland.org. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Three months ago, the city of Piedmont welcomed its new Climate Action Fellow, Emma Grossman. Over the next 11 months, she will be focused on helping the city meet its climate goals and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Grossman grew up in Seattle, Washington, surrounded by nature. She and her father would go camping and hiking in their spare time bonding over nature. Her love for the environment has become a huge part of who she is today. “From a very young age, I was taught to really love nature,” she said. “I see nature as a really intrinsic part of who I am, and that love has never gone away.” Grossman pursued her passion at New York University, where she graduated with degrees in environmental studies and global public health. It was at NYU where Grossman realized she could turn her love of nature into a career. “I think when I got to college, I realized that loving the environment was something that I could actually put into my work and become professionally important to me as well,” Grossman said. Grossman spent her college career working as a sustainability consultant and a food waste & recovery intern for companies in New York City. After graduation this past May, she found Piedmont’s fellowship through the Sustainability Service Corps and was drawn to the idea of working in government. Climate action fellow Emma Grossman in front of City Hall “I was immediately drawn to working for city governments. It’s something I really haven’t done before, but I had an inkling that I might like it,” Grossman added. “As I read through the city of Piedmont’s profile and their job description, it immediately caught my eye, and that went to number one on my list.” As a Climate Action fellow, her primary role is to assist in the implementation of Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan. A plan that was passed in 2018 to support statewide climate efforts and provide a pathway for Piedmont to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030, and be on track to reduce emissions 80% by 2050. “I’m mainly involved in our electrification strategy and decarbonization work,” Grossman added. She is the current lead on the rebate program in Piedmont, helping residents switch from fossil fuel-burning home appliances to electric. It’s only been three months, but she’s already making an impact on the program. “I took a look at the program and its reach in the last two years, and I made a report about that. We have some potential changes to the program coming soon, based on my recommendations and what we talked about as a department,” said Grossman. Over the remaining eight months of Grossman’s fellowship, she’ll be dedicated to helping Piedmont become a sustainable, green community. “I want residents to be able to experience the full benefits of electrification and of meeting our climate action goals,” she added, “I want residents to breathe healthier air, drink cleaner water, and experience cleaner parks.”
articles.title: Profile: Climate Action Fellow Emma Grossman

Profile: Climate Action Fellow Emma Grossman By Jake Lannon Three months ago, the city of Piedmont welcomed its new Climate Action Fellow, Emma Grossman. Over the next 11 months, she will be focused on helping the city meet its climate goals and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Grossman grew up in Seattle, Washington, surrounded by nature. She and her father would go camping and hiking in their spare time bonding over nature. Her love for the environment has become a huge part of who she is today. “From a very young age, I was taught to really love nature,” she said. “I see nature as a really intrinsic part of who I am, and that love has never gone away.” Grossman pursued her passion at New York University, where she graduated with degrees in environmental studies and global public health. It was at NYU where Grossman realized she could turn her love of nature into a career. “I think when I got to college, I realized that loving the environment was something that I could actually put into my work and become professionally important to me as well,” Grossman said. Grossman spent her college career working as a sustainability consultant and a food waste & recovery intern for companies in New York City. After graduation this past May, she found Piedmont’s fellowship through the Sustainability Service Corps and was drawn to the idea of working in government. Climate action fellow Emma Grossman in front of City Hall “I was immediately drawn to working for city governments. It’s something I really haven’t done before, but I had an inkling that I might like it,” Grossman added. “As I read through the city of Piedmont’s profile and their job description, it immediately caught my eye, and that went to number one on my list.” As a Climate Action fellow, her primary role is to assist in the implementation of Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan. A plan that was passed in 2018 to support statewide climate efforts and provide a pathway for Piedmont to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030, and be on track to reduce emissions 80% by 2050. “I’m mainly involved in our electrification strategy and decarbonization work,” Grossman added. She is the current lead on the rebate program in Piedmont, helping residents switch from fossil fuel-burning home appliances to electric. It’s only been three months, but she’s already making an impact on the program. “I took a look at the program and its reach in the last two years, and I made a report about that. We have some potential changes to the program coming soon, based on my recommendations and what we talked about as a department,” said Grossman. Over the remaining eight months of Grossman’s fellowship, she’ll be dedicated to helping Piedmont become a sustainable, green community. “I want residents to be able to experience the full benefits of electrification and of meeting our climate action goals,” she added, “I want residents to breathe healthier air, drink cleaner water, and experience cleaner parks.” ATLAS HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY Old Fashioned Service and High-Quality Installations www.AtlasHeating.com 510-629-6021

articles.text: Superintendent Jennifer Hawn delivered her second annual “State of the District” report at the Jan. 21 school board meeting. Hawn’s presentation outlined the strategic plan of the Piedmont Unified School District and highlighted the district’s recent focus on academic investment. “We have accomplished a lot, and we should just take a moment to just enjoy the fact that we have an incomparable team of administrators, of teachers, of classified staff. They provide expert service every day,” Hawn said. Hawn highlighted a significant change at the elementary level this year as a story of success. “We moved away from a curricular program, an English language arts program, that we didn’t feel really reflected that science of learning focus. And we moved toward Fish Tank learning, which is a new English language arts adoption,” she said. Creating an environment where students can thrive is another district priority. One metric the district uses to assess this is the California Healthy Kids Survey. Hawn said there were some inconsistent survey results at the middle school, which prompted a review of the school’s climate and culture. “Piedmont Middle School being named a California School to Watch this year is really exciting. There’s an award ceremony that will happen in March, and I’m just super excited to see PMS recognized for the great work that they do,” Hawn said. The Schools to Watch program is a national network of hundreds of schools in 20 states. Schools apply in the fall and submit an application following a validation visit. Piedmont Middle School was found to meet the program’s qualifications. Hawn also addressed the district’s cell phone policy, which she described as a work in progress. The district is currently implementing a one-year cell phone policy and plans to adopt a more restrictive permanent policy next year to align with state directives. “We made the bold and innovative move to adopt Latin, we are super excited about that,” Hawn said, referring to plans to introduce Latin to fifth graders next year. Hawn also reported strong interest in AP Business and Personal Finance, a new course to be added next year. Earlier in the evening, Elise Marks said that 130 students had expressed interest, which would require five separate course offerings. Hawn noted that reviewing and updating the district’s mathematics programming would be a focus in the near future. “Math has been a conversation. We have a [math] board policy that is actually out of date, so we really do need to take a look at math pathways,” Hawn said. “The secret sauce in Piedmont is really community engagement,” Hawn said when introducing the topic of partnering outside the classroom. Hawn said she has started holding “student lunches” this year so she can hear directly from students. The district has also placed a renewed focus on adding more meaningful field trips. Hawn acknowledged that there has been significant change in the district in recent years and signaled that the pace of change may slow. “We have accomplished a lot in the last several years, and so I think moving forward, a lot of the work that we’ll be doing is thinking about how we might refine what we are currently working on, rather than adding something significantly new,” she said. “I wish we could print this and put this in the Piedmont Post,” board member Susy Struble said following Hawn’s report. articles.text: Understanding dyslexia and language-based learning differences As a speech-language pathologist, one of the most common pieces of advice I hear given to struggling readers is well-intentioned but incomplete: “They just need to read more.” For many children, increased reading practice does help. But for a significant number of students, reading more—without the right support—only leads to frustration, fatigue, and declining confidence. The reason is simple: reading is not a natural skill. Unlike spoken language, which most children acquire through exposure, reading requires the brain to make very specific connections between sounds, letters, and meaning. When those connections don’t develop easily, practice alone is not enough. Dyslexia is one of the most well-known language-based learning differences. It is not a problem with intelligence or motivation. Children with dyslexia often have difficulty with phonological processing—the ability to hear, identify, and manipulate the sounds in spoken words. This makes learning sound-letter relationships and decoding words especially challenging. Other children may struggle with oral language skills, such as vocabulary, sentence structure, or understanding complex language. These students may learn to decode words but have trouble with reading comprehension, written expression, or retaining what they read. In both cases, telling a child to “just read more” is like asking someone to run farther without first teaching them how to walk efficiently. Why does more practice sometimes backfire? When reading is effortful, children expend so much mental energy decoding words that little is left for comprehension. Repeated failure can lead to avoidance, anxiety, and the belief that they are “bad readers.” Over time, this can affect academic performance across subjects and impact self-esteem. This is why some children read nightly, attend school faithfully, and still fall further behind. The issue is not a lack of effort: it’s a mismatch between the child’s learning needs and the instruction they are receiving. Research is clear about what supports struggling readers. Effective intervention is explicit, systematic, and structured. It targets the underlying skills that support reading, including phonemic awareness (hearing and manipulating sounds in words), sound-symbol relationships, decoding and encoding (reading and spelling), vocabulary and language comprehension, working memory and language organization. Approaches grounded in the science of reading help children build what researchers call orthographic mapping, the process by which words become stored in long-term memory for automatic recognition. Once this happens, reading becomes faster, smoother, and more enjoyable. Speech-language pathologists often play a key role in this process, particularly when reading difficulties are tied to broader language weaknesses. Intervention is most effective when it is individualized and based on a child’s specific profile of strengths and needs. If your child dislikes reading, avoids it, or seems to work much harder than peers, trust your instincts. More reading is helpful after the right skills are in place—not before. With proper assessment and evidence-based support, struggling readers can make meaningful progress and, just as importantly, regain confidence in their ability to learn. Reading success isn’t about trying harder. It’s about teaching smarter. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

But for a significant number of students, reading more—without the right support—only leads to frustration, fatigue, and declining confidence. The reason is simple: reading is not a natural skill. Unlike spoken language, which most children acquire through exposure, reading requires the brain to make very specific connections between sounds, letters, and meaning. When those connections don’t develop easily, practice alone is not enough. Dyslexia is one of the most well-known language-based learning differences. It is not a problem with intelligence or motivation. Children with dyslexia often have difficulty with phonological processing—the ability to hear, identify, and manipulate the sounds in spoken words. This makes learning sound-letter relationships and decoding words especially challenging. Other children may struggle with oral language skills, such as vocabulary, sentence structure, or understanding complex language. These students may learn to decode words but have trouble with reading comprehension, written expression, or retaining what they read. In both cases, telling a child to “just read more” is like asking someone to run farther without first teaching them how to walk efficiently. Why does more practice sometimes backfire? When reading is effortful, children expend so much mental energy decoding words that little is left for comprehension. Repeated failure can lead to avoidance, anxiety, and the belief that they are “bad readers.” Over time, this can affect academic performance across subjects and impact self-esteem. This is why some children read nightly, attend school faithfully, and still fall further behind. The issue is not a lack of effort: it’s a mismatch between the child’s learning needs and the instruction they are receiving. Research is clear about what supports struggling readers. Effective intervention is explicit, systematic, and structured. It targets the underlying skills that support reading, including phonemic awareness (hearing and manipulating sounds in words), sound-symbol relationships, decoding and encoding (reading and spelling), vocabulary and language comprehension, working memory and language organization. Approaches grounded in the science of reading help children build what researchers call orthographic mapping, the process by which words become stored in long-term memory for automatic recognition. Once this happens, reading becomes faster, smoother, and more enjoyable. Speech-language pathologists often play a key role in this process, particularly when reading difficulties are tied to broader language weaknesses. Intervention is most effective when it is individualized and based on a child’s specific profile of strengths and needs. If your child dislikes reading, avoids it, or seems to work much harder than peers, trust your instincts. More reading is helpful after the right skills are in place—not before. With proper assessment and evidence-based support, struggling readers can make meaningful progress and, just as importantly, regain confidence in their ability to learn. Reading success isn’t about trying harder. It’s about teaching smarter. articles.text: In spring, Piedmont Council’s five troops (youth groups for all kids, boys and girls, in 5th grade and up) open their doors to families interested in the scouting program. Open house meetings are an opportunity for kids and their parents to visit a specific scout troop, meet youth and adult leadership, and learn about that troop’s unique brand of scouting. Troops also share recent and upcoming activities. In advance of the troop’s open houses, Council leaders will host informational sessions during the week of February 9th. These sessions will explain the basics of the scouting program, talk about what scouting looks like in Piedmont, assist in deciding which troop to visit, and provide a safe space to have your questions about scouting answered. To receive information about the time and location of the info sessions, please fill out the Google form here: https://forms.gle/WwPS4SkHRhoEwuro6 Scouting is a time-honored tradition in the community of Piedmont, with twenty-percent of Piedmont youth involved in the program. Scouting provides youth with hands-on leadership experiences and allows them to practice life skills while serving their community. It instills citizenship and character, fosters communication, and builds a self-reliance in youth as they organize events and take on challenges together. Have questions about the info sessions or open houses? Reach out to Piedmont Council’s Program Coordinator Eris Turner: eturner@piedmontbsa.org – (510) 844-4752

articles.text: As the Lighting Ceremony in Piedmont Park approaches each year, Piedmont residents are invited to send holiday greetings to friends and neighbors through donations to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF). Contributions will be directed in accordance with donors’ wishes, supporting not only the replacement swings, but also the Dearing Family Memorial Project, and the Reforest Piedmont, Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood effort. PBF extends its heartfelt thanks to all who contributed and is pleased to recognize donors whose gifts were made since July 1, 2025. More than $200,000 has been received, which includes a generous bequest from long time community volunteer Carl Anderson. Special appreciation is also extended to the underwriters who financed the citywide mailing that invited the entire community to participate in the annual Piedmont Lights Up! event. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team continued its stature as one of the best teams in California with two wins at Binks Rawlings Gym over the past week. They recently beat Antelope 57-37 on Saturday, January 24 and won 76-55 over Alameda on Thursday, January 22. Their 20-point victory over Antelope was quite the statement. The Highlanders entered as the No. 16 ranked team in California while the Titans were ranked No. 18. Without star PHS point guard Jenelle Solis, who remains out with an ankle injury, the win represents a critical result toward Piedmont’s postseason seeding. “Everyone is continuing to grow. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont looks to pick itself up after tough losses to Alameda and University. Their loss to Alameda marked the fifth time they relinquished a fourth-quarter lead. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team had a frustrating week with two losses, bringing its record to 13-7 overall and 1-3 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division teams. They lost 67-58 to Alameda in the Hornets’ home gym on Thursday, January 22 and fell 83-62 to University at Binks Rawlings Gym two days later. Piedmont held a 53-46 lead with 3:30 left in the game with Alameda, but was held to five points in the remaining time. The loss marked the Highlanders’ fifth defeat after holding a fourth-quarter lead. “We’re 13-7, but easily could be 18-2,” said coach Ben Spencer. “We had five games where we had a fourth quarter lead; Acalanes, we had a 12 point lead with two minutes to go. Berkeley, we had a five point lead. Alameda, we had an eight point lead. We just haven’t found a way to close games.” Alameda and University had a common trend where the opponent’s press caused problems for the Highlanders’ offense. “The press seemed to give us a lot of trouble against Alameda. I thought we did well tonight against University’s press when we ran it correctly. University is just deep with 12 guys who are all great shooters. But, I’m proud of how we battled,” Spencer said. 12 to jump ahead 52-30. PHS crept closer in the third, 66-47, but University outscored Piedmont 17-15 in the final going. There were four lead changes in the first quarter. Lorin scored on a put-back offensive rebound to lead 8-6 after two minutes, but University went up 12-10 on its own offensive board a couple of minutes later. PHS then went ahead 15-14 after Will Hinman converted a pair of free throws with 56 seconds left, but University scored on its next possession on a 3-pointer. They never relinquished the lead from then on. articles.text: Beats San Leandro 3-1, falls 2-0 to top-ranked O’Dowd Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team is rolling through its final regular season matches, beating San Leandro 3-1 at Witter Field on Tuesday, January 20 while losing 2-0 at Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland on Friday, January 23. The results bring Piedmont’s record 6-2-4 (W-T-L). Despite the loss to O’Dowd, the Dragons are currently the No. 13 ranked team in California and No. 55 in the entire nation. Piedmont, meanwhile, is No. 174 in the state, making Friday’s result encouraging. Bishop O’Dowd is currently undefeated at 8-0-0 without conceding a single goal this year, and fields talented players like freshman Sadie Siedel, who competes semi-pro on Oakland Soul’s W League team. “We were very much looking forward to Bishop O’Dowd. They are a very good team and is a really good test to see where we’re at,” coach Matt Spencer-Harty said. Piedmont now has six matches left in its season against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division foes. In the buildup, Makenna Small sprung Ayla Blanford out wide down the left side around the midfield line. articles.text: This time of year, many people feel drawn to start fresh with fitness. Routines reset, motivation jumps, and the search for a new gym begins. But while it’s easy to find a gym or sign up for classes, it’s much harder to know what makes one fitness program more effective than others. Movement alone isn’t enough. To get real results, workouts need structure, purpose and progression. That’s where progressive resistance training comes in. Progressive resistance means gradually increasing the challenge placed on the body so it has a reason to adapt. That might look like lifting slightly more weight, performing an extra repetition, slowing a movement for better control, or improving balance and stability. When challenges increase over time, the body responds by building strength, lean muscle and resilience. A common misconception is that resistance training is only for “getting big.” In reality, progressive resistance is one of the most effective tools for a broad range of goals, including weight loss Small groups and hands-on coaching combined with a progressive program encourage consistency. Personalized coaching and the latest technology help people follow – and stick to – the program. and managing important health markers such as ApoB and insulin levels. Building lean muscle helps the body burn more energy throughout the day, improves blood sugar regulation and supports fat loss, without training like a bodybuilder. For most people, the result isn’t bulky muscles, but a stronger, leaner and more efficient body that supports lasting health. Research consistently shows that structured, progressive strength training outperforms unplanned workouts. Studies have found that people following progressive resistance programs gain 20 to 40 percent more strength and significantly more lean muscle than those performing similar exercises without planned progression. Effort matters, but direction matters more, especially when time to train is limited. Without progression, the body adapts and then stops changing. You may feel tired after workouts, but strength plateaus, muscle tone stalls and weight management becomes harder. Progressive resistance gives the body a clear reason to keep improving. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) exhibits the first major retrospective of painter Suzanne Jackson, entitled Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love, on display now through March 1. Organized in collaboration with the artist, the exhibition spans six decades of Jackson’s multifaceted career. Featuring more than 80 works, including paintings, drawings, and a new large-scale commission, the show explores Jackson’s novel approach to color, light, and structure, as well as her deep connection to nature, poetry, and performance. Jackson is known for her ethereal early canvases and her recent three-dimensional “floating” acrylic paintings that challenge traditional notions of painting. The exhibition also examines her interdisciplinary background as a dancer, poet, and theater designer, highlighting how these influences and her ties to radical artist communities shaped her art. “Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love promises to be a groundbreaking exhibition,” said Christopher Bedford, SFMOMA’s Helen and Charles Schwab Director. “Jackson continues to innovate by extending paint into three dimensions and embedding it with found materials to reflect on personal and cultural histories.” “Suzanne Jackson’s life has been driven by an insistent search for creative freedom and a bohemian spirit that is indebted to the San Francisco ethos in which she was raised,” added Jenny Gheith, curator of the exhibition and SFMOMA’s Interim Head of Painting and Sculpture. “What Is Love captures the curiosity, wonder and resilience of Jackson’s life’s work.” Visit sfmoma.org or call 415.357.4000 for more information. > edwardjones.com | Member SIPC Dreaming up the ideal retirement is your job. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company premieres a new production of Anton Chekhov’s classic play The Cherry Orchard tomorrow, Thursday, January 29. Directed by Carey Perloff, artistic director emerita of American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.), Chekhov’s final work centers on an aristocratic family facing the loss of its estate at the turn of the 20th century as debt threatens both their home and its famed cherry orchard. Despite looming foreclosure, the family resists practical solutions, clinging to tradition as social and economic change advances around them. Perloff returns to Marin Theatre after directing last season’s critically-acclaimed play Waste. In a press release, she said The Cherry Orchard remains one of Chekhov’s most radical plays, blending comedy and melancholy while examining why people resist necessary change. “The Cherry Orchard is one of the most radical and remarkable plays ever written about change,” Perloff said. “It’s about why change is crucial and why we always resist it. It’s incredibly funny and incredibly sad, full of narcissistic characters who are sure they’re the star of their own story, but fail to realize the damage they’re causing to the people around them. And it’s about how love is always irrational and surprising. I’m deeply grateful to Marin Theatre for giving all of us the chance to re-explore this big, juicy classic in light of our own times.” The production features a cast of Bay Area theater veterans and visiting New York actors. Lance The Cherry Orchard cast. Gardner, Marin Theatre’s executive artistic director, plays Yermolai Lopakhin, a former peasant turned businessman. Liz Sklar stars as Lyubov Ranevskaya, the indebted estate owner, with Anthony Fusco as her brother, Leonid Gayev. The cast also includes Danny Scheie, Leontyne Mbele-Mbong, Jomar Tagatac, Howard Swain, Joseph O’Malley, Rosie Hallett, Anna Takayo, Molly Ranson and Joel Morel. Photo by Chris Hardy Gardner said Chekhov’s characters are “profound and amusing,” describing them as nostalgic, hopeful and deeply flawed. The production uses Paul Schmidt’s translation. The Cherry Orchard runs January 29 through February 22 at Marin Theatre, 397 Miller Ave. in Mill Valley. Tickets range from $38 to $89, plus handling fees, and are available at MarinTheatre.org or by calling 415-388-5208.

articles.text: Gregory Porter Jazz vocalist and two-time Grammy Award winner Gregory Porter returns to Davies Symphony Hall for a concert drawing on music from across his career as well as new material from an upcoming album. Porter was raised in Bakersfield, California, where he was influenced by gospel music, church singing and the legacy of Nat King Cole. Before turning fully to music, he studied at San Diego State University and initially pursued athletics. He began performing professionally in San Diego jazz clubs in the early 2000s, building a reputation for his rich baritone voice and thoughtful songwriting. He achieved wider recognition with his debut album “Water” in 2010 and his 2012 album “Be Good.” Both recordings earned Grammy nominations and helped establish Porter as a leading voice in contemporary jazz. He achieved broader recognition with his Blue Note debut, “Liquid Spirit,” which won the Grammy Award for best jazz vocal album in 2014 and became a commercial and critical success. Porter won a second Grammy in the same category for “Take Me to the Alley” in 2017. In addition to his original work, Porter has been widely praised for his interpretations of jazz standards. His 2017 tribute album, “Nat King Cole & Me,” paid homage to one of his earliest influences. Porter has toured internationally and performed at major jazz festivals and concert halls around the world. Porter has since received additional Grammy nominations for “Nat King Cole & Me” and for 2020’s “All Rise.” His work blends jazz with soul and gospel elements, a style shaped by his upbringing and early experiences singing with his family in community and church settings. He has toured internationally and performed at major concert halls and jazz festivals, earning praise for expanding the reach of jazz while remaining grounded in its traditions. The concert, presented by SFJAZZ, begins at 8 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/25-26/gregory-porter/ for more information and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet celebrates the work of choreographer and “Father of American Ballet” George Balanchine, with a specially-curated program presented in February featuring three of his signature ballets performed over a weeklong run. The program highlights Balanchine’s role in shaping ballet in the United States and offers audiences multiple opportunities to attend performances and related events throughout the week. Performances include “Diamonds,” “Serenade” and “Stars and Stripes,” tracing Balanchine’s development as a choreographer and his influence on American ballet, and are scheduled from February 10 through February 15 with evening and matinee options. “Diamonds,” set to music by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, reflects Balanchine’s grounding in classical ballet and Russian tradition. “Serenade,” his first ballet created in the United States, is also set to Tchaikovsky and is widely regarded as a landmark work that helped establish a distinctly American ballet style. The program concludes with “Stars and Stripes,” a work set to music by John Philip Sousa that incorporates marches and patriotic themes. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Ballet The program highlights Balanchine’s role in shaping ballet in the United States. Performances begin at 7:30 p.m. on February 10, 11 and 12, and at 8 p.m. on February 13. Matinee performances are scheduled for 2 p.m. on February 14 and 15, with an additional evening performance at 8 p.m. on February 14. Post-performance activities will take place in the War Memorial Opera House lobby on select nights. Square dancing accompanied by Evie Ladin and her string band is scheduled following the February 10 and February 13 performances. Line dancing hosted by Sundance Saloon will follow performances on February 11, 12, 14 and 15. In addition to the performances, a panel discussion is scheduled for Tuesday, February 10, prior to opening night. The discussion will feature artistic director Tamara Rojo and author Elizabeth Kendall, whose books focus on Balanchine’s career and influence. The conversation will be moderated by James Steichen, author of “Balanchine and Kirstein’s American Enterprise.” Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/balanchine/ to learn more and to purchase tickets.

Saturday, January 31, 7:00 p.m. Cristiana Pegoraro Solo Piano Concert The incomparable Italian piano master Cristiana Pegoraro returns once more to Piedmont for another recital, as always supporting her work runniing an arts academy in Narni, Italy. The President of Narnia Arts Academy and the Artistic Director of Narnia Festival, hailed by the New York Times as “an artist of the highest caliber,” Italian-born pianist Cristiana Pegoraro has performed on the world’s most prestigious stages, including Lincoln Center, Carnegie Hall, the United Nations (New York), the Sydney Opera House, Festspielhaus (Salzburg), Musikverein (Vienna), Royal College of Music (London), Auditorium Parco della Musica (Rome), Teatro alla Scala (Milan), and many others, and at music festivals throughout the world. He holds a B.S. in Music from Florida A&M and a Master of Music in Flute Performance from Wayne State. William has toured extensively in Japan with Kyodo Tokyo and regularly works as a soloist, collaborator, and recording artist. He started playing the flute at age 11, saying the flute chose him, and has stayed with it because of the beautiful form of communication it offers, the opportunity to share in a cherished art form, and the deep lessons of confidence and growth he encountered at a young age. Dr. Carl Blake, a local piano master who has performed worldwide to constant acclaim, has happily introduced Will to the best of the Bay Area, often playing together as a duo exploring piano and flute repertoire. This concert is free to all, and donations are welcome. articles.text: The pleasures of an innovative story ballet , P PI IE ED DM MO ON NT T, , C CA A 9 94 46 61 11 1 lies in his path -including the heart of a provincial girl Tatiana Larin; the engagement of her sister Olga; and the life of Olga’s groom Lensky, whom he kills in a duel. He finally gets himself broken when Tatiana, transformed by time and an advantageous marriage, turns away from his belated declaration of love, even as she acknowledges the persistence of her youthful feelings. Unlike many 19th century novels, where lovers are often victims of class or circumstance, the failed romance of Eugene Onegin is a matter of wrong choices and poor timing, particularly on Onegin’s part. Unable to feel deeply, he fails to recognize the real thing—Tatiana’s sincere and passionate love; when the epiphany finally arrives, it comes too late. This realistic core is what keeps the story relevant to modern sensibilities, in a world where formal obstacles to happy love stories are largely gone. The key to unhappiness, the Onegin confirms, is often hidden in ourselves. Adapting a novel in to ballet is hard. Its main currency— words—cannot be used in dance. Adapting poetry (Pushkin’s Onegin is written as a novel in verse) is harder still. Not only do you have to convey that complexity without words, but a choreographer also has to translate the poem’s rhythm, tone, and narrative intelligence into movement. In that regard, Possokhov’s Onegin is a stunning success. With a choice of scenes, the emotional intelligence of the dancers’ interpretation, and the innovative use of multimedia effects, Possokhov renders the novel’s core while steadily raising the emotional stakes for both performers and audience without losing narrative clarity. Among the ballet’s most intense sequences is Tatiana writing her letter, an iconic moment for anyone who has read the novel, in which she boldly confesses her love for Onegin, only to be rejected. Danced in the Saturday, January 24 performance by Max Cauthorn and Nikisha Fogo, the scene unfolds as a masterful crescendo of emotion. Their pas de deux begins with Tatiana leading, buoyed by the exhilaration of first love, and ends with her crushed by Onegin’s cool lecture on emotional restraint. Tatiana’s final gesture—a graceful folding of her hands over her face—is a rending moment that Fogo handles with precision and tenderness. Tatiana’s vivacious sister, Olga Larina (Isabella De Vivo), and the romantic Vladimir Lensky (Victor Prigent) are equally compelling: Lensky in the famous solo preceding the duel, where he reflects on love and fate, and Olga in the aftermath of her groom’s death, when she relinquishes her mourning black scarf after being courted by dashing officers. In her case, at least, youth and life win out and carry her away dancing. In contrast to the complexity of human feeling at the ballet’s center, the spirits of nature—who in Possokhov’s telling mark the changing seasons—provide some of the production’s most delightful interludes, as well as an opportunity to showcase the company’s roster of gifted young dancers. © San Francisco Ballet © San Francisco Ballet, photo by Lindsey Rallo Katherine Barkman and Joseph Walsh in Possokhov’s Eugene Onegin Their costumes, flaming red and orange in summer and icy blue in winter, were designed by Academy Award-winner Tim Yip (of Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon fame) whose imaginative flair and theatrical precision shape the visual world of the ballet. Yip’s work is especially effective in the two ball scenes, which alternate between the simpler styles of the Larin country estate and the taffetas and formal wear of the imperial ball in St. Petersburg. His designs are particularly arresting in Tatiana’s dream sequence, where her premonition of Lensky’s death unfolds as a phantasmagoria of animal figures: dancers wearing full sculptural animal heads, including a bear that resolves into Onegin, reminiscent of The Nutcracker’s Mouse King but far more unsettling, transforming the stage into a waking nightmare. The staging amplifies the ballet’s emotional force. Set design by Tom Pye is paired with Jim French’s lighting and Finn Ross’s projections, creating immersive environments that enhance Possokhov’s choreography. Several of Pushkin’s verses are projected onstage and underscored by a voiceover. In the final act, a vivid red backdrop gives way to a swirling storm, snow falling from above in a visual echo of Onegin’s inner turmoil. Elsewhere, metaphors are used with precision: a raven projected onto the curtain suddenly takes flight, and Onegin’s recurring black coach comes to symbolize his restless, unmoored existence. The resulting effect is brisk and cinematic, while staying true to the classical ballet language. To this drama, Ilya Demutsky’s original score provides an ideal frame, weaving Onegin’s unsettling, foreboding motifs with Tatiana’s youthful hopefulness, growing gravitas, and capacity for love. Given that Eugene Onegin is inseparable, for many audiences, from Tchaikovsky’s beloved opera score, the bar for this commission was considerable. Demutsky rises to the challenge, creating a score that gives the ballet a musical voice of its own without overwhelming it. Eugene Onegin is a bold opening note for the Company’s 93rd season, the third under the artistic leadership of Tamara Rojo. Judging by this performance, the season is her most ambitious ever, setting a tone that favors narrative clarity, emotional intelligence, and theatrical imagination as highly as technical rigor and expressive dancing for which San Francisco Ballet is known. Eugene Onegin will be onstage at the War Memorial Opera House until February 1. articles.text: Historic Buena Vista Winery was built in 1857 Buena Vista Winery in Sonoma, California holds a remarkable place in American wine history. It is one of the oldest premium wineries in the state, founded in 1857 by the intrepid Count Agoston Haraszthy. Often considered the “father of California viticulture,” Haraszthy was an Hungarian immigrant, adventurer, and visionary who brought European winegrowing ambition to the young American West. He established Buena Vista at a time when Napa and Sonoma were hardly known for wine at all. He believed California had the potential to rival the great vineyards of Europe, and he spared no effort in importing hundreds of vinifera grape varieties and innovating early wine production techniques. The winery’s early years were as colorful as its founder: Haraszthy’s life spanned roles as a sheriff in Southern California, a pioneer of modern viticulture, and a tragic figure whose death in Nicaragua, falling into a river and being devoured by an alligator, became part of wine lore. Through boom, bust, phylloxera, and Prohibition, Buena Vista endured — though not without interruptions. In the 20th century, the estate passed through various owners, and much of its historic site fell into disrepair before renewed interest in its legacy emerged. In May 2011, Jean-Charles Boisset and the Boisset Family Estates acquired Buena Vista Winery, marking a new era for the storied property. Boisset’s family winery group — rooted in Burgundy, France and known for crafting wines around the world — brought fresh energy, respect for heritage, and investment to restore Buena Vista’s historic structures, including its mid- 19th-century press house and underground wine caves. Under his stewardship, Buena Vista blends tradition with modern hospitality, positioning the estate as both a tribute to California’s wine pioneers and a vibrant tasting destination. Today, visitors can explore Buena Vista’s historic press house, experience guided tastings, and enjoy exhibits that illuminate its role in American wine history. articles.text: Eleanor Moore, 94, of Piedmont, California, passed away peacefully on October 23, 2025. A devoted wife, mother, grandmother, and beloved member of her community, Eleanor will be remembered for her kind spirit, her radiant smile, and her unwavering optimism. Born on January 24, 1931, in San Jose, California, Eleanor was the second child of William Bailey and Ethel Hjelm. She grew up in Lompoc, California alongside her older brother Earl. When she was just 5 years old, the unexpected passing of her father, left her and her brother to be raised by their devoted mother, a school teacher. Eleanor attended Lompoc High School and graduated from UCLA with a degree in geography, a field that reflected her fascination with travel, cultures and the wider world. Following a memorable mother-daughter graduation trip to Europe — traveling by train and boat — she returned to Lompoc, where she married James Moore, the brother of her best friend from high school. After their wedding, Jim worked in the Bay Area and Eleanor relocated to Oakland, eventually moving to Piedmont in 1964. Together, they raised two children, Bill and Marilyn. Their partnership was grounded in love, laughter and shared adventures, and they enjoyed a wonderMerritt Peralta Foundation where she was a board member, as well as the East Bay Zoological Society Foundation and the Cancer League. She was a member of the Claremont Country Club, the Bellevue Club, and the Piedmont Community Church. Eleanor also enjoyed engaging her mind as a member — and often treasurer — of various investment clubs, where her keen interest in the stock market met her sharp intellect. Yet, no matter how busy her calendar, she always found time for bridge, travel, and time with family and friends. An avid traveler, Eleanor and Jim visited all seven continents together, collecting memories, friendships and stories along the way. Eleanor is survived by her son Bill Moore (Monica Cardoni), her daughter, Marilyn Moore Weber, and her three grandchildren: Jim and John Weber and Shannon Moore. She is predeceased by her husband Jim, her brother Earl and her son-in-law Bill Weber. Kind, generous, and adventurous, Eleanor brightened every room she entered. Her example of empathy, honesty, and grace will remain a lasting legacy to all who knew her. A private service was held in her honor. Since the late 20th century, many women have embraced strength training for its visible benefits—a leaner, stronger physique. What wasn’t fully understood at the time were the far broader effects of progressive strength training on long-term health. Studies conducted over the past thirty years have shown that regular strength training can also: • Increase metabolic efficiency • Improve glucose control and insulin sensitivity • Support brain health and cognitive function • Enhance focus, mood, and resilience Today, many health and fitness professionals consider strength training a non-negotiable foundation of healthy aging. Yet one crucial question lingered for years: Could post-menopausal women safely gain these benefits, especially when it comes to bone health? The answer is a clear and confident YES. The science confirms that progressive strength training—when combined with impact training (activities such as controlled jumping and firm landings)— places healthy stress on bones, stimulating ossification (bone formation). A couple of important studies brought this into focus: • A 2011 randomized controlled trial found that post-menopausal breast cancer survivors who engaged in moderate-intensity resistance training plus impact training improved both lumbar spine bone density and lean muscle mass, compared to a low-intensity stretching group. • The landmark LIFTMOR study (Australia, 2017) took a bolder approach, testing an eight-month, supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training program in post-menopausal women with low bone mass. Participants experienced significant gains in lumbar spine bone mineral density, femoral neck (hip) bone strength, and functional strength and balance. Importantly, these benefits occurred even without hormone replacement therapy. The takeaway is powerful and encouraging: Women of all ages— including peri- and post-menopausal women—can safely build strength, protect their bones, and enhance long-term health through progressive strength and impact training. As with all training, outcomes are influenced by nutrition, genetics, hormone levels, post-exercise recovery practices, and other factors. Mia Honore and Mark Sutro founded CRUfit Montclair in 2013. CRUfit offers a diverse mix of group classes, small group training and personal training to meet the fitness needs of all ages. A stolen white 2011 Mitsubishi Lancer was being pursued by OPD patrol vehicles following an armed high jacking with a rifle. The vehicle was first reported in the area of Pacific Avenue at 4:00 a.m. and then continued onto Highland and down Wildwood to Palm. OPD authorized the use of road spikes by PPD officers but the suspect did not go onto the street with the tack strips. The stolen vehicle eventually turned onto El Cerrito and attempted to enter Witter Field at the El Cerrito gate, which was locked. The vehicle became wedged under the gate and the driver fled on foot. The suspect, Carleton Ferguson, was apprehended and arrested by OPD at 4:16 a.m. He was charged with carjacking, possession of a firearm, and evading police. The rifle was recovered and a female passenger was detained. The driver was taken to a hospital.
